findings.issue_text: [BUG] updateEvent's fallback branch evaluates event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId) inside the branch where externalCalendarId is already falsy, so the search compares externalIds against a null/undefined key, always returns undefined, and calendar.events.update is invoked with calendarId: undefined. Rescheduling any booking whose stored reference lacks externalCalendarId (every booking created through the no-credentialId destination branch, which passes no externalId to CalendarManager.createEvent) fails the Google update with a missing/invalid-calendarId error that CalendarManager swallows as a failure result, leaving the Google event at the old time while the Cal.com booking and attendee emails show the new time.

[BUG] deleteEvent uses the same dead fallback — find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId) when externalCalendarId is already falsy — so calendarId is always undefined for references without an externalCalendarId. Canceling such a booking throws inside calendar.events.delete (caught and logged), and the event stays on the host's Google calendar after cancellation, complete with its conferencing link, while Cal.com frees the slot — ghost events for attendees and double-booked time for the host.

[BUG] The no-credentialId branch calls createEvent(c, event) without the third externalId argument that the credentialId branch passes (createEvent(credential, event, destination.externalId)), so CalendarManager returns externalId: undefined and EventManager persists booking references with no externalCalendarId. Bookings whose destinationCalendar rows lack a credentialId store calendar references that Google's update/delete falsy-externalId fallbacks cannot resolve, permanently breaking reschedule and cancellation for exactly those bookings — the previous code stored evt.destinationCalendar.externalId on every reference.

[BUG] createEvent resolves the target calendar exclusively via destinationCalendar.find((cal) => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId with a 'primary' fallback, so a destination calendar without a credentialId matches nothing and the event is created on the credential's primary calendar instead of destinationCalendar.externalId. For every destinationCalendar row with a null credentialId, events silently relocate from the user's selected calendar (the old code used destinationCalendar.externalId directly) to the account's primary calendar, and the resulting reference stores no externalCalendarId, which then triggers the update/delete failures above on the next reschedule or cancel.

[BUG] createEvent builds the Graph events URL from mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId — the first destination calendar — while EventManager now invokes createEvent once per host credential, so every host's token targets the first host's calendar id. Collective bookings with multiple Office 365 hosts (the exact case this PR adds) POST to /me/calendars/{firstHostCalendarId}/events with each secondary host's token; Graph returns 404 for a calendar outside that host's mailbox and the event is never created on the secondary host's calendar, leaving their slot booked in Cal.com but empty on their calendar.

[BUG] In updateAllCalendarEvents, credential is declared once outside the per-reference loop and only reassigned when the in-memory filter or the DB lookup finds a match, so an unresolvable reference.credentialId leaves the previous iteration's credential in place when result.push(updateEvent(credential, ...)) runs. Rescheduling a multi-reference collective booking after one host deleted their calendar credential (or their credential row has no app slug) reuses the previous host's credential, attempting the update against the wrong user's Google/Microsoft account — 404ing on the mismatched uid/calendarId or mutating the wrong account — instead of failing that single reference.

[BUG] createEvent (and createAttendees at lines 161-166) resolves calendarId from the first element of event.destinationCalendar only, ignoring which host's credential the event is being created for. Multi-host collective bookings create all Lark events in the first host's selected calendar — duplicated when the tenant app token has access, or rejected with permission errors for every other host's credential — while each other host's own selected calendar stays empty.

[BUG] BaseCalendarService.createEvent filters every credential's calendar list against mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId — the first destination calendar — on every create call, regardless of which host's credential is in use. For multi-destination collective events, a secondary host's CalDAV/Apple credential contains none of the first host's calendar URLs, so the filter yields an empty calendar list and no event is created on that host's calendar at all — the collective multi-host fix silently no-ops for every non-first CalDAV host.

[BUG] createEvent sets the Google organizer attendee email from the first destination calendar's externalId (mainHostDestinationCalendar) even when selectedCalendar was resolved to a different host's calendar by credentialId. In the multi-host collective case this PR introduces, each secondary host's Google event is created advertising the first host's calendar address as organizer, misattributing the organizer in attendee UIs and misrouting Google's attendee-response handling for those events.

[BUG] evt.destinationCalendar is assigned null when neither eventType nor organizerUser has a destination calendar, so the optional-chained evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars) silently discards every teammate's collected destination calendar. Collective events whose organizer has no selected destination calendar — the default configuration for users who never picked an installed-app calendar — skip the multi-host calendar creation this PR exists to deliver; teammates' selected calendars are ignored and their events fall back to primary calendars.

[BUG] updateEvent reuses the same first-destination-calendar organizer email, re-stamping mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId onto the event payload on every update regardless of which host's calendar is being targeted. Every reschedule of a multi-host collective booking rewrites secondary hosts' Google events to list the first host's calendar address as the organizer, misattributing the organizer on each reschedule of exactly the bookings this feature targets.

[BUG] Inside the new per-reference loop, the recurring-cancellation path still resolves each remaining booking via updBooking.references.find((ref) => ref.type.includes("_calendar")), taking only that booking's first calendar reference. Canceling a recurring collective booking deletes each remaining occurrence only from the first host's calendar — and re-attempts that same deletion once per outer reference, duplicating delete calls — leaving every secondary host's calendar populated with events for occurrences the organizer canceled.

[BUG] The new catch block returns calendarReference?.map(...) ?? [], which is an empty array for any error thrown before calendarReference is assigned (e.g., the newBookingId lookup at the top of the try). A prisma/DB failure during reschedule now resolves to an empty result list that callers treat as 'no calendar references to update', so the reschedule completes in the database without any calendar update and without the success:false failure entry the old catch returned — the failure signal is gone.

[ADVISORY] Three hand-rolled copies of the fetch-credential-from-DB fallback now exist — createAllCalendarEvents (here), updateAllCalendarEvents (~505), and handleCancelBooking.ts (~424) — and they already drift: the two EventManager copies include the app relation and construct appName, while the cancellation copy fetches the bare credential with no app data. A DB-fetched credential in the cancellation path resolves through a different code path than the same credential at creation/reschedule time (no app slug available where the others construct appName), and any change to credential resolution — e.g., honoring the invalid flag, which all three copies pass through unchecked — must be replicated in three places or the flows diverge further.

[ADVISORY] Only evt.destinationCalendar[0] is connected to the booking's single destinationCalendar relation, so the multi-host destination list computed at creation is discarded from persisted state. Every later flow rewritten in this diff (cancel, confirm, editLocation, requestReschedule, webhooks) rebuilds the event from booking.destinationCalendar with only the first host's destination, so any fallback keyed on evt.destinationCalendar — Google's organizer email, Lark's calendarId fallback when a reference lacks externalCalendarId — can only ever resolve the first host's calendar for the life of the booking.

[ADVISORY] CalendarEvent.schedulingType is added to the contract and populated in handleNewBooking (schedulingType: eventType.schedulingType) but no code in this diff reads it. The event payload grows a field with no consumer — either the per-provider multi-calendar dispatch that motivated it was left out of this PR, or it is dead contract surface the next maintainer has to reverse-engineer; deleting it changes nothing in this diff.

[BUG] EventManager.create destructures `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? []` and then reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` unguarded, so a null or empty-array destinationCalendar throws instead of triggering the documented Cal Video fallback. A booking or confirmation with location integrations:google_meet and no destinationCalendar — the exact case the fallback comment describes, and now the null emitted by handleNewBooking and the [] emitted by confirm.handler/editLocation — throws TypeError "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')" and fails the request, where the old `?.` code silently fell back to Cal Video.

[BUG] Office365CalendarService.createEvent resolves the target calendar from destinationCalendar[0] (mainHostDestinationCalendar) and ignores both the per-credential destination and the new externalId argument, so every per-host invocation from createAllCalendarEvents targets the first host's externalId. For a collective booking with multiple Office365 hosts, host #2's event is created via `/me/calendars/{host#1's calendarId}/events` using host #2's token — Microsoft returns 404 and the additional host never receives a calendar event, while the booking proceeds; the PR's headline multi-host fix silently holds only for Google.

[BUG] LarkCalendarService.createEvent (and createAttendees) resolve calendarId from destinationCalendar[0] regardless of which host's credential is performing the creation. Collective bookings with multiple Lark hosts attempt host #2+'s creation against host #1's calendarId with the wrong tenant credential, the Lark API rejects it, and additional hosts end up with no calendar event for the booking.

[BUG] The prisma booking write connects only `evt.destinationCalendar[0]`, permanently discarding the additional team hosts' destination calendars that evt carries for collective events. requiresConfirmation and payment-gated collective bookings create their calendar events later from the persisted single destination calendar (confirm.handler, Stripe and PayPal handlePaymentSuccess all rebuild evt from booking.destinationCalendar), so team hosts never get calendar events — the multi-host fix silently vanishes on every deferred-creation flow.

[BUG] The slug spread was rewritten from `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` to `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})`, inverting the flag condition on an unrelated file in this PR. Deployments with IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED=false now create organizations with no slug at all (org routing/lookup by slug breaks, or Prisma rejects the write), while billing-enabled orgs get slug set immediately, bypassing the requestedSlug moderation flow the old code implemented.

[BUG] updateEvent's fallback `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId` only executes when externalCalendarId is falsy, so it searches for a calendar whose externalId equals a falsy value — dead code that can never match and always yields undefined. Any reschedule/location edit on a booking whose calendar reference lacks externalCalendarId (every reference produced through the new no-credentialId branch stores result.externalId = undefined) calls events.update with calendarId undefined; googleapis throws "Missing required parameter: calendarId", the error is swallowed by the catch, and the user's Google event is never updated.

[BUG] deleteEvent contains the same dead find — when externalCalendarId is falsy the find can never match, so calendarId resolves to undefined instead of falling back to the event's destinationCalendar as the old code did. Cancelling a booking whose calendar reference has no externalCalendarId throws "Missing required parameter: calendarId" inside events.delete, leaving the Google event orphaned on the user's calendar after cancellation.

[BUG] createEvent selects the calendar via `find(cal => cal.credentialId === credentialId)?.externalId` and falls back to "primary" whenever no destinationCalendar matches the creating credential, while CalendarManager still returns destination.externalId as the reference's externalId. Bookings created through the supported no-credentialId path (destinationCalendar.credentialId null) now land on the credential's primary calendar instead of the configured destinationCalendar.externalId, and because the reference stores destination.externalId, later updates/deletes 404 and the primary-calendar event is orphaned.

[BUG] The recurring-event cleanup block was moved inside the new per-reference loop but still sweeps all `bookingToDelete.user.credentials` across all updatedBookings and only `.find`s each updated booking's first calendar reference, ignoring the loop's own reference. Cancelling a recurring collective booking (which now has multiple calendar references) runs the full deletion sweep once per reference — duplicate deleteEvent calls that error on the second pass — and the sweep only iterates the organizer's credentials, so remaining occurrences stay on team hosts' calendars and only the first reference of each updated booking is ever deleted.

[BUG] The merge-delete still uses `booking.references.find((reference) => reference.type.includes("_calendar"))` even though the same function was converted to process all calendar references, so only the first calendar reference's event is deleted. Reschedule-with-merge (the newBookingId path) of a multi-reference collective booking leaves stale events on every host after the first, orphaning those calendar entries with no error surfaced.

[BUG] evt.destinationCalendar is set to null when neither the event type nor the organizer has a destination calendar, and the later `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` silently no-ops on null. A collective event whose organizer lacks a destination calendar but whose members have them collects the members' calendars into teamDestinationCalendars and then discards them, so no calendar event is created for any member host.

[BUG] Multi-host destination calendar collection is gated on `eventType.schedulingType === "COLLECTIVE"`, which dynamic multi-user links (user1/user2 booking URLs) never satisfy, even though the TODO this diff removes explicitly named "dynamic collective events" as a case to handle. Dynamic group bookings still create calendar events only on the first user's destination calendar — the requirement the deleted comment acknowledged is silently dropped by this fix.

[BUG] BaseCalendarService.createEvent filters the credential's calendars against destinationCalendar[0]'s externalId, which cannot match any additional host's CalDav/Exchange/Apple calendar. Per-host creation for collective bookings filters to an empty calendar list on every host after the first and resolves with no created event, so CalDav/Exchange/Apple Calendar hosts silently receive no events while the booking reports success.

[BUG] createEvent (and the mirrored code in updateEvent) stamps the organizer email as destinationCalendar[0]'s externalId on every host's copy, so events created on additional hosts' Google calendars claim the first host's calendar address as organizer. Every non-first host's event copy carries first-host organizer metadata — attendees and hosts see the wrong organizer on those copies and each reschedule rewrites the same wrong value via updateEvent.

[ADVISORY] The only verification change in the entire diff is a single updated literal (`destinationCalendar: []`) in the BOOKING_REJECTED payload expectation — the diff's only test file contains no coverage of the new behavior it ships. The per-destination creation loop, the DB credential fallback, Google's find-by-credentialId selection, and multi-reference update/delete have no test in the diff (scanned: apps/web/playwright/webhook.e2e.ts is the only test-shaped file touched), so regressions like the dead-code find in updateEvent ship to production with no CI signal, and the new array shape of BOOKING_CREATED/CANCELLED payloads is unasserted anywhere.

[ADVISORY] The hand-repeated `x ? [x] : y ? [y] : []` destinationCalendar conversion is duplicated across nine handlers with no shared helper and has already drifted between copies. This site drops the user.destinationCalendar fallback every sibling keeps, and handleNewBooking's variant emits null instead of [] — the exact drift that feeds the EventManager.create TypeError — so the next handler author copies whichever variant they find first and inherits its particular gap.

[ADVISORY] The ~20-line "fetch credential from DB and map appName" block is hand-duplicated in createAllCalendarEvents, again in updateAllCalendarEvents, and in a divergent third variant in handleCancelBooking that omits the app include and appName mapping both EventManager copies perform. The three hand-maintained copies have already drifted (the cancel path's fetch lacks the app relation the EventManager copies deem necessary to resolve the calendar service), so any future change to credential resolution must be applied in three places and will miss the divergent one — biting collective hosts whose calendar events silently stop being deleted.

[BUG] The Google Meet fallback dereferences the destructured first element without optional chaining (`mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration`), so it throws TypeError whenever evt.destinationCalendar is null or []. A booking with Google Meet location and no destinationCalendar (organizer/eventType both without one — handleNewBooking assigns null on lines 1063-1067, and the paypal/stripe/confirm handlers assign []) crashes with 'Cannot read properties of undefined (reading integration)' instead of falling back to Cal Video — the exact no-Google-calendar case this guard was written for.

[BUG] The rewrite `...(!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` → `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` inverts when slug is written, in a file with no connection to the PR's destinationCalendar intent. With team billing disabled (self-hosted installs), organizations are now created with no slug at all, breaking org URL routing; with billing enabled, slug is written directly at creation, bypassing the requestedSlug approval flow the unchanged isOrganizationVerified:false logic presumes — all hidden inside a calendar-fix PR.

[BUG] updateEvent's fallback branch runs `.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` only when externalCalendarId is falsy, so the predicate can never match and the fallback always yields undefined where it previously returned destinationCalendar.externalId. Rescheduling any booking whose calendar reference lacks externalCalendarId (every booking created through the no-credentialId destination path in this diff) sends calendarId: undefined to calendar.events.update, which throws the missing-required-parameter error — the Google event is never moved to the new time.

[BUG] deleteEvent's fallback has the same dead predicate — searching for a destination whose externalId equals the falsy externalCalendarId — so calendarId is always undefined when the reference lacks externalCalendarId. Cancelling such a booking throws in calendar.events.delete (missing calendarId), leaving the event stranded on the user's Google calendar after the booking is gone.

[BUG] createEvent resolves the target calendar only via `destinationCalendar.find(cal => cal.credentialId === credentialId)`, so a destinationCalendar row with null credentialId — the legacy case createAllCalendarEvents still explicitly serves through its no-credentialId branch — never matches and the write silently degrades to calendarId 'primary'. Users whose configured destination calendar predates credentialId get new events created on their primary Google calendar instead of the selected destination calendar, with no error anywhere.

[BUG] The reference mapping takes externalCalendarId from result.externalId, but createAllCalendarEvents' legacy branch calls createEvent(c, event) without passing destination.externalId, so references for credential-less destinations are now stored with no externalCalendarId (previously evt.destinationCalendar.externalId); the identical edit sits at lines 208-209. Bookings created through a destinationCalendar without credentialId become un-updatable and un-cancellable on the correct calendar: their stored reference has no externalCalendarId and GoogleCalendarService's update/delete fallbacks are dead code, so reschedule and cancel of those bookings fail.

[BUG] `evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars)` is a no-op when evt.destinationCalendar is null (the assignment on lines 1063-1067 explicitly produces null when neither eventType nor organizer has a destination), silently discarding every collected member destination calendar. A COLLECTIVE booking whose organizer has no destination calendar but whose team members do never creates events on the members' calendars — the exact multi-host scenario this PR claims to fix — with no error logged anywhere.

[BUG] createEvent (and the createAttendees/updateEvent/deleteEvent fallbacks) read only destinationCalendar[0]'s externalId, so for a multi-host collective event every per-credential call targets the first host's Lark calendar regardless of which member's credential is authenticated. A collective booking with two Lark hosts makes host B's authenticated createEvent call write to host A's calendarId (failing or duplicating) while host B's destination calendar never receives the event — the multi-host fix is implemented only for Google.

[BUG] createEvent builds the events URL from only destinationCalendar[0].externalId, ignoring which member's credential the service instance authenticates as. For a multi-host collective booking with Office365 hosts, each per-destination createEvent call posts to /me/calendars/{first-host-externalId}/events under the other hosts' tokens — targeting the wrong host's calendar or 404ing — so members' own destination calendars never receive the event.

[BUG] The CalDAV base createEvent filters the user's calendars against only mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId (the first array element), so a non-first host's service instance finds no matching calendar for a multi-host collective event. For collective bookings whose hosts use Apple/CalDAV-type calendars, the non-first hosts' createEvent calls match zero calendars and silently create nothing — their destination calendars never receive the event.

[BUG] The recurring-event deletion fan-out (all user calendar credentials × all updatedBookings) now executes once per calendar reference inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop even though each iteration re-derives the same uid/externalCalendarId from the updated bookings' own references. Cancelling a recurring collective multi-host booking with N calendar references runs the identical deletion fan-out N times: each event is deleted once and then re-deleted N-1 times, generating guaranteed already-deleted API errors that the surrounding try/catch swallows, wasting provider API quota and flooding logs with false failures.

[BUG] The merge path still resolves the old event's calendar reference with a single `.find(...)` even though this diff introduces bookings that carry multiple calendar references. When a multi-host collective booking is rescheduled through the merge path (newBookingId), only the first host's old calendar event is deleted and the remaining hosts' stale events stay on their calendars.

[ADVISORY] The PR rewrites loadUsers wholesale — new dynamicUserList validation, a try/catch remapping errors to HttpError 400/500, and a Prisma select that drops the previous `organization: { select: { slug: true } }` — none of which is traceable to the destinationCalendar multi-host fix. Anyone approving this PR as a calendar fix silently signs off on changed user-loading semantics for every booking: empty/missing dynamicUserList now aborts with 500 'Unable to load users' instead of returning an empty list, server-side Prisma known-request errors are re-reported as client 400s, and any consumer of the loaded users' organization.slug on the dynamic-link path now reads undefined.

[ADVISORY] The catch block of the calendar-update method drops `console.error(message)` without any replacement, returning failure EventResults in complete silence. Operators investigating 'the reschedule didn't update my Google/Office365 event' lose the only server-side breadcrumb this path produced; failures that escape CalendarManager's internal handling (e.g. the new prisma.credential.findUnique rejection) now leave no trace.

[ADVISORY] The multi-host destination state exists only in memory: the Booking row persists a single destinationCalendar via `connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id }`, so only the first host's destination survives creation. Every downstream flow in this very diff that rebuilds evt from the booking row — bookingReminder cron, handleCancelBooking, confirm/editLocation/paypal handlers — constructs a one-element array from booking.destinationCalendar, so the multi-host destination set is enforced only during create and is unrecoverable later except by reverse-engineering booking references.

[BUG] updateEvent's fallback branch searches destinationCalendar for an entry whose externalId equals externalCalendarId, the very variable that is guaranteed falsy inside that branch, so the fallback always evaluates to undefined instead of the previous destinationCalendar.externalId. Any updateEvent call without an externalCalendarId (legacy booking references, plus new references created via the integration-fallback branch which now store undefined externalCalendarId) passes calendarId: undefined to googleapis, the call rejects, and reschedules fail to move the Google event, leaving users double-booked on their calendar.

[BUG] deleteEvent has the same self-contradictory fallback — find(cal => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId) inside the branch where externalCalendarId is falsy — so calendarId is always undefined when the reference carries no external calendar id. Cancelling a booking whose reference lacks externalCalendarId calls calendar.events.delete with calendarId undefined, the API call throws, and the calendar event survives cancellation, leaving ghost events on hosts' calendars.

[BUG] LarkCalendarService.createEvent (and createAttendees at 161-166, updateEvent at 189-194, deleteEvent at 234-239) ignores the new per-credential routing and always uses event.destinationCalendar[0], so every destination other than the first is created against the organizer's calendar id. When EventManager processes a secondary Lark host's destination for a collective booking, the Lark API is called with the first host's (possibly Google or another user's) externalId, the call fails and is swallowed by CalendarManager's catch, and that host silently never receives the calendar event — the exact multi-host scenario this PR claims to fix.

[BUG] Office365CalendarService.createEvent builds the events URL from destinationCalendar[0].externalId regardless of which credentialId is being processed, so collective bookings write secondary hosts' events against the first destination's calendar id. For a collective booking with an Office365 host beyond the first, the request goes to /me/calendars/{organizer's calendar id}/events under the host's credentials and 404s; the error is caught and logged, the host's calendar never receives the event, yet the booking reference still records the host's externalId as the event's location so later updates target an event that was never created.

[BUG] BaseCalendarService.createEvent filters the credential's discovered calendars down to those matching destinationCalendar[0].externalId, so when the CalDAV service belongs to any destination other than the first the filter matches nothing and no event is created anywhere. Collective bookings with a CalDAV host whose destination is not first produce zero events for that host while CalendarManager still returns success and a reference row is written with the uid, creating a phantom reference that later updates and deletes will fail against.

[BUG] updateCalendarEvents declares credential outside the per-reference loop, never resets it per iteration, and omits the if (credential) guard that the create path (line 363) has, so a reference whose credentialId cannot be resolved reuses the previous reference's credential or calls updateEvent(undefined, ...). A calendar reference pointing to a deleted or app-less credential updates the wrong host's calendar using another reference's uid and externalCalendarId, or throws a TypeError inside getCalendar that aborts every remaining reference in the loop via the catch block, failing the whole reschedule.

[BUG] The update flow's BookingReference payload now reads externalCalendarId and credentialId from result.externalId/result.credentialId, but CalendarManager.updateEvent was never extended to return either (only createEvent's return gained them in this diff) and the old evt.destinationCalendar fallbacks were deleted, so both fields are undefined for every calendar-type result. Reschedules produce calendar references with no calendar coordinates; wherever these payloads are persisted (the newBookingId merge path writes reference rows for the new booking) the new references lack credentialId/externalCalendarId, degrading those bookings to the legacy all-credentials sweep and Google's dead-find fallback, which then fails the API call on every later update or cancel.

[BUG] createEvent now selects the target calendar solely via find(cal => cal.credentialId === credentialId) with a 'primary' fallback, dropping the old destinationCalendar.externalId selection, so destination rows with a null credentialId never match. Users with pre-refactor DestinationCalendar rows (null credentialId) get events created on their primary calendar instead of the calendar they selected, and the EventManager fallback branch then creates one event on the primary of every matching same-provider credential, producing duplicate calendar events where the old code produced one.

[BUG] The recurring-cancellation path, now executed once per calendar reference, still resolves each updated booking's calendar reference with find() (first match only) and sweeps all of bookingToDelete.user.credentials, discarding the per-reference calendarCredential it just resolved from the DB. Cancelling one instance of a recurring collective booking deletes only the first calendar reference of every remaining booking — secondary hosts' events linger on their calendars — while the identical all-organizer-credentials sweep is repeated once per reference, multiplying duplicate delete API calls; hosts' own credentials are never used for their recurring events.

[BUG] evt.destinationCalendar is initialized to null when neither eventType nor organizerUser has a destination calendar, so the subsequent evt.destinationCalendar?.push(...teamDestinationCalendars) is a silent no-op that drops every team host's destination calendar. Collective bookings whose organizer never configured a destination calendar ignore all team members' selected destination calendars; createAllCalendarEvents falls back to creating on the organizer's credentials (Google: their primary), so hosts' chosen calendars never receive the event.

[BUG] The outgoing booking webhook payload's destinationCalendar field changed shape from object-or-null to array — the e2e expectation update from destinationCalendar: null to destinationCalendar: [] in this diff is direct evidence — an unversioned breaking change to webhook subscribers. Installed apps and subscriber endpoints that parse destinationCalendar.externalId now read undefined off an array and silently misroute, so every existing webhook subscriber breaks on deploy with no version bump or compatibility path.

[ADVISORY] The Calendar interface now mandates a credentialId routing parameter that TypeScript lets implementers silently ignore (fewer-parameter implementations are legal), and three of the four implementations in this diff (Lark, Office365, BaseCalendarService) do ignore it, so the boundary cannot enforce the per-credential destination selection it was added to guarantee. The next calendar provider — or any future edit to the non-Google implementations — compiles cleanly while creating events on the wrong calendar, which is the exact bug class shipped in this PR, because the contract's key parameter is unenforceable at the interface.

[ADVISORY] createAllCalendarEvents awaits each destination's createEvent sequentially in a for-loop on the booking-creation hot path while the sibling no-credentialId branch (line 377) fans out with Promise.all. Collective bookings pay one full external calendar API round-trip per host in series (hundreds of milliseconds to seconds each), so booking confirmation latency grows linearly with host count and multi-host team bookings become visibly slow.

[ADVISORY] The new DB-credential fallback is hand-duplicated three times (createAllCalendarEvents here, updateCalendarEvents at ~505-527, handleCancelBooking at ~432-441) with already-divergent rules — both EventManager copies require credentialFromDB.app?.slug while handleCancelBooking's copy fetches without the app include and accepts any credential. The same legacy credential (one with no App row) resolves in the cancel path but is silently dropped in the create/update paths, so such hosts' calendars never receive collective events with no error surfaced; the next change to credential resolution must be made in three drifting places.

[BUG] The Google-Meet fallback dereferences mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration with no nil guard, but this PR itself produces events whose destinationCalendar is null (handleNewBooking `: null`) or [] (payment webhooks `: []`), so the destructured value is undefined and `.integration` throws. EventManager.create() crashes with TypeError before any event is created: booking a Google-Meet event type whose organizer/eventType has no destinationCalendar returns a 500 instead of falling back to Cal Video, and Stripe/PayPal handlePaymentSuccess throws after the customer has already been charged.

[BUG] The slug condition was silently inverted from `!IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug }` to `IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {}` — an unrelated behavior change smuggled into a destinationCalendar PR with no acceptance. With IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED=false, Organization.create runs without the required unique slug and the insert fails, breaking organization creation entirely; with it true, unverified organizations immediately occupy their slug, bypassing the requestedSlug verification flow the adjacent line (153) still implements.

[BUG] updateEvent's fallback branch calls `event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)` only when externalCalendarId is falsy, so the predicate compares externalId against null/undefined, never matches, and the destinationCalendar fallback that previously returned event.destinationCalendar.externalId is now dead code. Rescheduling/updating any booking whose calendar reference has a null externalCalendarId (legacy reference rows, or references written by this PR's no-credentialId creation path) sends calendarId: undefined to calendar.events.update, so the Google event keeps the stale time while the booking appears successfully rescheduled.
